extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and practitioners building or using humor detection/scoring datasets (especially for Spanish/Twitter)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, extracting and crowd-annotating a corpus of Spanish tweets for humor recognition and funniness scoring, including sampling, annotation UI, quality control and aggregation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus size and balance target
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of the extraction and annotation process was to build a corpus of at least 20,000 tweets that was as balanced as possible between the humor and not humor classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted at least 20k tweets; design sampling and injection strategies to approach class balance between humorous and non-humorous examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of data (humorous accounts and realtime samples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract tweets from selected accounts and from realtime samples: fifty humorous accounts (random sample size 12,000) and realtime Spanish tweets (random sample size 12,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mixture of curated humorous-account samples and unbiased realtime language-filtered samples to avoid source bias; additional injections from humorous accounts (4,500) were used when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language detection for data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: The language detection feature is provided by the Twitter REST API.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Twitter's language field when fetching tweets to restrict to Spanish-language tweets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion criteria for tweets
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignored retweets, responses, citations and tweets containing links, as the text should be self-contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude items that depend on external context (links, replies, retweets) to ensure the tweet text alone can be judged for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding source bias in negative samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred realtime tweet samples because selecting certain negative examples (news, inspirational thoughts) could bias the non-humorous class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building non-humorous samples, avoid over-representing a narrow set of subgenres (e.g., news) that would make classification trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation interface simplicity and minimal instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Tried to keep the user interface as intuitive and self-explanatory as possible, trying not to induce any bias on users and letting them come up with their own definition of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design UI to be simple and friendly to keep annotators engaged; provide minimal prescriptive definitions to avoid biasing their notion of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit humorous intent question
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly asking the annotator if the text intends to be humorous makes the distinction between the Not Humorous and Not Funny classes less ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate 'is this intended to be humorous?' (Yes/No) from 'how funny is it?' to reduce class ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation choices and funniness scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators are asked whether the tweet intends to be humorous. The available options are 'Yes', 'No' or 'Skip'. If the annotator selects 'Yes', five emoji are shown so the annotator can specify how funny he considers the tweet. The emoji also include labels describing the funniness levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a ternary initial decision (Yes/No/Skip) with a 1–5 ordinal funniness rating for 'Yes' responses; graphical emoji with labels can improve clarity vs. star ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow skip and help options
rubrics_metrics.description: We also allowed to skip a tweet or click a help button for more information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide 'Skip' and easily accessible help to avoid forcing low-quality labels when annotators are unsure or confused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation session test tweets for quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: The first tweets shown to every session were the same: three tweets for which we know a clear answer (one of them was humorous and the other two were not). These 'test tweets' were meant as a way of introducing the user into how the interface works, and also as an initial way for evaluating the quality of the annotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present known-answer test items at session start both to train the annotator on UI expectations and to flag low-quality contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtering low-quality annotator sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: When compiling the final version of the corpus, we considered the annotations of users that did not answer the first three tweets correctly as having lower quality. These sessions should not be used for training or testing machine learning algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude or mark annotations from sessions that fail the initial test tweets rather than using them in training/testing splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target annotations per tweet and prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: We first aimed to have five votes for each tweet, and to decide which tweet was humorous by simple majority. Tweets with three non-humorous annotations were considered as not humor and deprioritized so users could focus on ambiguous tweets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for multiple annotations per instance (target = 5); prioritize showing tweets with fewer annotations; deprioritize items already classified decisively to allocate annotator effort to ambiguous instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision and aggregation rules (humor label and funniness score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple majority of votes for categorizing between humorous or not humorous, and weighted average for computing the funniness score only for humorous tweets. The scale goes from one (Not Funny) to five (Excellent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate intent with majority vote; compute an ordinal-weighted mean for funniness, but only for items labeled humorous by majority. Be explicit about how ties and undecided cases are treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of ties and undecided cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Under this scheme, 27.01% of the tweets are humorous, 70.6% are not-humorous while 2.39% is undecided (2.38% tied and 0.01% no annotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and preserve undecided/tied cases rather than forcing a label; treat them separately in analysis or downstream tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merging duplicate tweets' annotations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some tweets with more than six annotations because we merged annotations from a few dozen duplicate tweets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect duplicate tweet instances and merge their annotations to consolidate judgments for the unique content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Session-level deduplication via web session info
rubrics_metrics.description: The tweets were randomly chosen but web session information was kept to avoid showing duplicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep client/session identifiers to avoid presenting the same tweet multiple times to a single annotator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting: exclude outliers (test tweets) from counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Each tweet received 3.8 annotations on average... not considering the test tweets as they are outliers (they have a large number of annotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting annotation distribution metrics, exclude intentionally over-annotated test items to avoid skewing statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-annotator agreement measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Used the Krippendorff's alpha measure: alpha value on humorous versus non-humorous is 0.5710. For funniness (ordinal) alpha is 0.1625 using a generic distance function between ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Krippendorff's alpha for any number of raters; treat intent as nominal and funniness as ordinal (use appropriate distance function). Interpret alpha scores with established thresholds (e.g., Fleiss) and report both nominal and ordinal agreement separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subset selection for subjectivity studies
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a subset of a thousand tweets with at least six annotations that could be used to study people's opinion on the same instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and use subsets with higher annotation counts when analyzing subjective phenomena (e.g., funniness distributions, disagreement patterns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset structure and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset consists of two CSV files: tweets (identifier and origin) and annotations (tweet identifier, session identifier, date and annotation value). Tweet text is not included in the corpus due to Twitter Terms and Conditions; they can be obtained from the IDs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release IDs plus annotation metadata when constrained by platform T&C; provide clear schema for CSV files and instructions for retrieving text from source platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling skew in annotator contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotator distribution was skewed: a few annotators labeled many tweets while most labeled few; the top 100 annotators contributed >70k annotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report annotator contribution distribution and consider its effects (e.g., concentrated annotator influence) on dataset biases and agreement measures; optionally analyze agreement on heavy annotators separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting collection process when annotation bias appears
rubrics_metrics.description: At a certain stage we noticed that the users were voting too many tweets as non-humorous... we made some adjustments: considered tweets with three non-humorous annotations as not humor and deprioritized them; injected 4,500 more tweets from humorous accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor class-frequency drift during annotation and adapt sampling/injection/prioritization strategies to reach desired balance and annotation utility.
